cards.statement: Error Identification (Level A) requires authors to describe an automatically detected input error in text.
cards.explanation: Error Identification (Level A) calls for text that identifies the affected input and describes the error, helping users understand what went wrong.

cards.statement: A text field's `aria-label` alone satisfies Labels or Instructions (Level A) for users reading the screen.
cards.explanation: Labels or Instructions (Level A) calls for guidance presented to users. An aria-label supplies naming text for assistive technology, rather than a visible label or instruction.
cards.misconception: An accessible name alone supplies the guidance that this criterion expects users to perceive.

cards.statement: Error Suggestion (Level AA) calls for known correction advice when authors automatically detect input errors.
cards.explanation: Error Suggestion (Level AA) asks authors to provide known ways to correct detected errors, unless doing so would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.

cards.statement: Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data) (Level AA) requires a confirmation page before a user submits a payment.
cards.explanation: Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data) (Level AA) permits reversible submissions, checks with correction, or review and confirmation. A confirmation page is one option.
cards.misconception: Covered financial submissions need a confirmation page even when another permitted safeguard exists.

source.title: Understanding SC 3.3.4: Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data)

cards.statement: On Input (Level A) lets a select navigate on change when authors provide advance warning to its users.
cards.explanation: Under On Input (Level A), authors advise users of the context change before they use the control. A notice beside the select can explain that choosing an option opens another page.

cards.statement: Setting `aria-required="true"` alone makes the browser automatically block an empty text input's form submission.
cards.explanation: On supported native controls, required participates in HTML constraint validation. aria-required communicates a requirement to assistive technology and adds no validation behavior.
cards.misconception: aria-required activates the browser's native missing-value validation.

source.title: ARIA: aria-required attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: A `<legend>` within a `<fieldset>` gives related form controls a shared group label.
cards.explanation: fieldset groups related controls, and its legend identifies the group, such as an address type. This gives the controls a shared context beyond their individual labels.

cards.statement: A clear placeholder can replace a text field's visible label under MDN's accessibility guidance.
cards.explanation: MDN advises using placeholder text as a brief hint, rather than a label replacement. The hint disappears as users enter a value, so it cannot preserve the field's identifying guidance.
cards.misconception: A sufficiently clear placeholder is an acceptable substitute for a field label.

source.title: placeholder HTML attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: Authors can meet Identify Input Purpose (Level AA) for eligible HTML fields with suitable `autocomplete` tokens.
cards.explanation: Identify Input Purpose (Level AA) accepts suitable autocomplete tokens as purpose metadata for eligible fields. These tokens communicate the kind of personal information the user enters.

cards.statement: Identify Input Purpose (Level AA) includes a field where users enter another person's birthday.
cards.explanation: Identify Input Purpose (Level AA) covers listed input purposes when fields collect information about the user. A field for another person's birthday falls outside that scope.
cards.misconception: A listed input purpose falls within this criterion even when the field collects another person's data.

cards.statement: MDN advises authors to defer `aria-invalid="true"` for an empty required field until form submission.
cards.explanation: For a required field, MDN advises setting aria-invalid="true" in response to validation, rather than merely because the initial value is empty.

source.title: ARIA: aria-invalid attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: WAI-ARIA 1.2 lets user agents expose `aria-errormessage` for a control with `aria-invalid="false"`.
cards.explanation: An aria-errormessage relationship is pertinent when aria-invalid="true". User agents must suppress that relationship when aria-invalid is false.
cards.misconception: The error-message relationship remains exposed regardless of the control's validity state.

cards.statement: Authors choose an informative image's text alternative according to its role in the surrounding content.
cards.explanation: Describe the information an informative image contributes in its context. A literal description of its appearance may miss why the image is on the page.

cards.statement: ARIA in HTML maps the decorative markup `` to the presentation role.
cards.explanation: The empty alt in this markup marks the image as decorative. ARIA in HTML assigns presentation semantics to this case because the image has no other naming source.

cards.statement: HTML-AAM names `` "Summary".
cards.explanation: HTML-AAM takes an image's name from nonempty alt ahead of title. The title attribute supplies a fallback name when the alt attribute is absent.
cards.misconception: An image's title attribute overrides a supplied alt when computing its accessible name.
cards.volatilityNote: HTML-AAM is a Working Draft; its published image-name computation may change.

source.title: HTML Accessibility API Mappings 1.0: img Accessible Name Computation

cards.statement: The WAI tutorial recommends "Printer icon" as the alternative for an image that serves as a Print button.
cards.explanation: A functional image's alternative identifies its action or destination, such as "Print". Describing the object alone misses the control's purpose.
cards.misconception: A functional image needs an alternative describing the pictured object rather than the action it performs.

cards.statement: The WAI tutorial treats a chart's short identifying `alt` as a sufficient alternative to its detailed data.
cards.explanation: WAI pairs a short description identifying a complex image with a longer text equivalent of its essential information, including important data and relationships.
cards.misconception: A short chart identifier conveys the detailed information needed for a complex image's alternative.

cards.statement: Authors may treat an informative CSS background image as exempt from Non-text Content (Level A).
cards.explanation: Non-text Content (Level A) covers meaningful visual information regardless of how the author inserts it. CSS backgrounds need an equivalent way to convey that information.
cards.misconception: Rendering meaningful information as a CSS background removes the text-alternative obligation.

cards.statement: Authors can give an inline SVG graphic an accessible name through its child `<title>` element.
cards.explanation: An SVG title provides naming text for its parent graphic. This child element conveys a short alternative that user agents can expose to assistive technology.

source.title: SVG title element - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: The WAI technique uses `role="img"` and an accessible name to identify a meaningful icon-font glyph.
cards.explanation: An icon font supplies a visual glyph. The WAI technique gives its containing element image semantics and a name to convey the icon's intended meaning.

source.title: Semantically identifying a font icon with role="img"

cards.statement: Images of Text (Level AA) permits an image of text when users can customize it to their requirements.
cards.explanation: Images of Text (Level AA) has a Customizable exception. It applies when users can change the image text's visual presentation to suit their needs.

cards.statement: For an image CAPTCHA, Non-text Content (Level A) treats a purpose label as a complete text-alternative solution.
cards.explanation: For CAPTCHA, Non-text Content (Level A) requires purpose-identifying text plus alternative CAPTCHA forms using different sensory modes, accommodating different disabilities.
cards.misconception: Identifying a CAPTCHA's purpose fulfills the criterion without providing alternative sensory forms.

cards.statement: Authors can replace synchronized captions with a transcript under Captions (Prerecorded) (Level A).
cards.explanation: Captions (Prerecorded) (Level A) calls for synchronized captions for prerecorded audio in video. A separate transcript lacks that synchronization; clearly labeled media alternatives for text are excepted.
cards.misconception: A separate transcript is interchangeable with synchronized captions for this criterion.

cards.statement: Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded) (Level A) permits a complete text alternative for a video.
cards.explanation: Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded) (Level A) accepts a text alternative conveying the visual and auditory information in sequence, including equivalents for any interaction.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.2.3: Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded)

cards.statement: Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) sets a 4.5:1 floor for paragraph text outside its exceptions.
cards.explanation: Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) compares text with its background. Meeting the threshold helps users with reduced contrast sensitivity read the text.

cards.statement: Under Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA), bold text qualifies as large-scale based on font weight alone.
cards.explanation: Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) uses both weight and size: at least 14 point for bold text or 18 point for other text, or equivalent sizes for CJK fonts.
cards.misconception: Bold font weight makes text eligible for the large-scale category regardless of its size.

cards.statement: Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) uses unrounded computed ratios when authors assess text contrast.
cards.explanation: Threshold comparisons use the computed ratio's full precision. Rounding a result for display does not make a below-threshold contrast ratio pass.

cards.statement: Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) exempts the text of a logo whose colors follow its brand identity.
cards.explanation: Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) exempts logo text whose appearance follows the brand identity. The Understanding guidance excludes low contrast added as an author's styling choice.

cards.statement: Contrast (Enhanced) (Level AAA) applies its 7:1 threshold to large-scale text as well as body text.
cards.explanation: Contrast (Enhanced) (Level AAA) sets 7:1 for ordinary text and 4.5:1 for large-scale text. Large text has its own threshold.
cards.misconception: The enhanced threshold for ordinary text also applies to large-scale text.

cards.statement: Non-text Contrast (Level AA) sets 3:1 for an active checkbox's state mark when authors style that mark.
cards.explanation: Non-text Contrast (Level AA) evaluates the mark needed to recognize a checkbox state against adjacent colors. The requirement concerns visual identification, not decorative parts.

cards.statement: Authors may use hue alone to distinguish success from failure under Use of Color (Level A).
cards.explanation: Use of Color (Level A) calls for another visual cue, such as text or a symbol, when hue communicates a status. Users need a way to identify that status beyond hue.
cards.misconception: Distinct hues are sufficient to communicate which status represents success and which represents failure.

cards.statement: Resize Text (Level AA) lets authors use browser zoom for the 200 percent text enlargement requirement.
cards.explanation: Resize Text (Level AA) allows browser zoom when users can double text size without losing content or functionality. Captions and images of text are exceptions.

cards.statement: Reflow (Level AA) bases its narrow-layout test on a device's physical screen width of 320 pixels.
cards.explanation: Reflow (Level AA) uses 320 CSS pixels for vertically scrolling content, rather than hardware pixels. Content needing a two-dimensional layout, such as a data table, is excepted.
cards.misconception: The reflow width refers to physical screen pixels rather than CSS viewport pixels.

cards.statement: Text Spacing (Level AA) tests a page's initial CSS spacing rather than the effects of user spacing changes.
cards.explanation: Text Spacing (Level AA) checks for lost content or functionality when users apply the specified spacing overrides. It does not dictate the page's default spacing.
cards.misconception: The criterion checks authors' default spacing rather than resilience to user-specified spacing.

cards.statement: Content on Hover or Focus (Level AA) requires authors' hover popups to stay visible as the pointer enters them.
cards.explanation: The Hoverable condition in Content on Hover or Focus (Level AA) supports moving the pointer onto the added content, for example to inspect a tooltip with magnification.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.4.13: Content on Hover or Focus

cards.statement: A disabled button's label remains subject to the text threshold in Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA).
cards.explanation: Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) exempts text that is part of an inactive user interface component. A disabled button's label falls under the Incidental exception.
cards.misconception: Text in a disabled control follows the contrast threshold for text in active controls.

cards.statement: A screen reader may announce changes in an `aria-live="off"` region while focus is inside that region.
cards.explanation: MDN describes off as limiting update announcements to a region that contains focus. The precise spoken behavior depends on the browser and assistive technology.
cards.volatilityNote: Actual announcements depend on evolving browser and assistive-technology behavior.

source.title: ARIA live regions - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: By default, WAI-ARIA 1.2 gives the `alert` role an implicit `aria-live="assertive"` value.
cards.explanation: An alert carries assertive live-region semantics even when the author omits aria-live. The role marks a message needing immediate attention.

cards.statement: In WAI-ARIA 1.2, the `status` role gives its updates the implicit `aria-live="assertive"` priority.
cards.explanation: WAI-ARIA 1.2 gives status an implicit aria-live="polite" value. Its default priority suits advisory updates rather than urgent interruptions.
cards.misconception: The status role requests assertive live-region handling by default.

source.title: ARIA: status role - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: In WAI-ARIA 1.2, the `timer` role gives its updates the implicit `aria-live="polite"` priority.
cards.explanation: WAI-ARIA 1.2 gives timer an implicit aria-live="off" value. Routine elapsed-time or remaining-time updates therefore start with that live-region setting.
cards.misconception: A timer implicitly requests polite live-region handling for its changing value.

cards.statement: For a live region, `aria-atomic="true"` requests presentation of its complete content after a relevant change.
cards.explanation: aria-atomic="true" instructs assistive technology to include the region's full content, rather than just the changed portion. It controls the scope of an update presentation.

source.title: ARIA: aria-atomic attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: By default, `aria-relevant` includes removal events among the live-region changes marked for notification.
cards.explanation: aria-relevant defaults to "additions text", covering added nodes and text changes. Authors include "removals" or "all" when they want deletions treated as relevant.
cards.misconception: Removing content counts as a relevant live-region update under the default aria-relevant setting.

source.title: ARIA: aria-relevant attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: MDN recommends creating a live region before authors insert the update they want announced.
cards.explanation: Declare the live region before an update and give assistive technology time to register it. MDN calls inclusion in the initial markup the most reliable approach.
cards.volatilityNote: Live-region registration and update announcements vary as browsers and assistive technologies evolve.

source.title: ARIA live regions - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: Status Messages (Level AA) expects authors to automatically focus messages so assistive technology detects updates.
cards.explanation: Status Messages (Level AA) requires programmatic identification that lets assistive technology present a status update without moving focus. Taking focus is not the mechanism it specifies.
cards.misconception: A status announcement depends on moving keyboard focus to the updated message.

cards.statement: Pause, Stop, Hide (Level A) accepts a user pause control for a continuously auto-scrolling sidebar.
cards.explanation: Pause, Stop, Hide (Level A) covers automatic movement lasting over five seconds alongside other content. Authors provide a pause, stop or hide mechanism unless the movement is essential.

cards.statement: A Stop button exempts a flashing banner from Three Flashes or Below Threshold (Level A).
cards.explanation: Three Flashes or Below Threshold (Level A) limits flash frequency or demands staying below the general flash and red flash thresholds. A stop control does not establish safe flashing.
cards.misconception: A user-operated Stop control exempts flashing content from the flash-safety criterion.

source.title: Understanding SC 2.3.1: Three Flashes or Below Threshold

cards.statement: Animation from Interactions is a Level AA requirement for interface motion triggered by user actions.
cards.explanation: Animation from Interactions is Level AAA. It addresses disabling motion animation triggered by interaction, except when that animation is essential to the function or information.
cards.misconception: Disabling interaction-triggered motion animation is a Level AA requirement.

cards.statement: Authors may replace a sliding transition with an opacity effect when `prefers-reduced-motion` is `reduce`.
cards.explanation: MDN interprets reduce as a request to remove, reduce or replace motion-based animation. An alternative effect can convey the same information while reducing distracting movement.

source.title: prefers-reduced-motion CSS media feature - MDN Web Docs
